question.prompt:
Circle \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) each have radius \(1,\) and the distance between their centers is \(\tfrac12.\) Circle \(C_3\) is the largest circle internally tangent to both \(C_1\) and \(C_2.\) Circle \(C_4\) is internally tangent to both \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) and externally tangent to \(C_3.\) What is the radius of \(C_4?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2023_AMC_12A_Q18_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
The equal outer radii help us locate the centers of the inner circles. Let \(O_1,O_2\) be the centers of \(C_1,C_2\), and let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(O_1O_2\). Then \(O_1M=O_2M=\tfrac14\).

A circle of radius \(0<s<1\) lying inside and tangent to both unit circles has a center \(P\) satisfying
\[
PO_1=PO_2=1-s.
\]
Thus \(P\) lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(O_1O_2\). By the Pythagorean theorem,
\[
(1-s)^2=PM^2+\frac1{16}\ge\frac1{16}.
\]
Since \(1-s>0\), we obtain \(s\le\tfrac34\). A circle centered at \(M\) with radius \(\tfrac34\) does satisfy both internal tangencies, so this is \(C_3\).

Now let \(N\) and \(r\) be the center and radius of \(C_4\). Internal tangency again puts \(N\) on the same perpendicular bisector, with \(NO_1=1-r\). External tangency to \(C_3\) gives \(MN=\tfrac34+r\). The right triangle \(O_1MN\) therefore gives
\[
\frac1{16}+\left(\frac34+r\right)^2=(1-r)^2.
\]
Expanding makes the \(r^2\) terms cancel:
\[
\frac58+\frac32r+r^2=1-2r+r^2,
\qquad
\frac72r=\frac38.
\]
Hence \(r=\tfrac3{28}\).

This radius is positive and less than 1. Choosing \(N\) on either side of \(M\) with \(MN=\tfrac67\) gives \(NO_1=NO_2=\tfrac{25}{28}=1-r\), so both reflected placements satisfy all the tangencies. The radius is \(\boxed{\tfrac3{28}}\), choice D.
solutions.title: Tangency distances and a right triangle
